column3: Crisis calling followed by turning away and disbelief parallels refusal of the faith call.
The warning against miserly or excessive spending does not clarify the focus's call, disbelief, or judgment.
The Fire calls those who turned away, reversing the focus's refused call to faith into final summons.
Its test of whether invoked beings hear a call only broadly relates to receiving the call to faith.
It immediately specifies the focus charge: when God alone was invoked, they disbelieved.
Faithful striving is a clear positive counterpart to the focus's refusal of faith and ensuing condemnation.
Calling powerless beings besides God exposes the misdirected devotion underlying disbelief in the true call.
The proclamation of one God and invitation to submit states the faith-call the focus says was refused.
The messenger explicitly calls people to believe in their Lord, directly matching the focus's earlier call to faith.
Disbelievers see the event they had invoked and their faces darken, a judgment-time counterpart to later remorse.
It rejects worship of those called besides God and commands submission to the Lord of the worlds.
Divine judgment of self-purification lightly contrasts with the self-directed hatred disclosed in the focus.
At final separation, people admit they ruined themselves through temptation, doubt, and false hopes.
The disciples' response of faith and submission provides the positive alternative to rejecting God's call.
A caller summons people to a dreadful event, paralleling the focus's final public address.
It directly joins disbelief with God's mqt and loss, supplying the focus's central divine condemnation.
The same judgment sequence explains punishment through arrogant, groundless worldly exultation.
The creation of the self does not clarify refusal of faith or the later exchange of condemnations.
It uses God's mqt for grave moral inconsistency, sharpening the severity of the mqt in the focus.
The believer's call to salvation against a call to Fire directly frames the alternatives behind the focus.
Groundless dispute and arrogance are called greatly hateful to God, closely illuminating the focus's mqt.
Love of faith and aversion to disbelief supply a direct moral opposite to the focus's response.
Human stinginess with divine stores does not develop the faith call, self-reproach, or final judgment.
General just recompense does not add a distinct connection to the focus's refused call and self-hatred.
It restrains self-praise before God's knowledge, a limited contrast to the focus's final self-condemnation.
God's true promise and universal return establish the judgment horizon in which the focus's address occurs.
Wrongdoers plotting against themselves offers only a broad self-incurred-consequence parallel.
Turning people from faith and dying in disbelief are linked to nullified deeds and abiding Fire.
The ease of resurrection provides only general background for the focus's final accountability.
The hidden reward for believers does not clarify the focus's account of rejected faith and remorse.
The final return for judgment distinguishes those who follow faith from those who disbelieve.
Calling on God with sincere devotion directly supplies the faithful answer to the focus's rejected call.
At judgment, false objects of prior calling vanish and disbelievers disown their former invocation.
The prohibition on social mockery and insult does not clarify the focus's final self-reproach.
God's knowledge of inner selves and forgiveness for returners is only a limited contrast to final self-hatred.
The self-reproaching soul gives a close internal counterpart to the focus's self-directed hatred.
Disbelievers hear the call as empty sound, directly explaining failure to receive the call to faith.
It rejects the false object of calling, affirms return to God, and identifies the excessive with the Fire.
Those called besides God possess no authority, exposing the false devotion opposed to faith in God.
It explicitly contrasts choosing disbelief over faith with the believer's required allegiance.
Demanding a sign from a messenger offers only a general instance of resistance to a prophetic call.
Noah's open calling supplies a broad model of prophetic invitation without the focus's response or outcome.
Arrogant rejection of God's signs meets humiliation at death, closely anticipating final condemnation.
God alone judges in truth while those called besides Him cannot judge anything.
Noah's continuous calling of his people gives a sustained prophetic counterpart to the refused call.
Its comparison of creation magnitudes only lightly supports the focus's judgment perspective.
The provision of safe travel routes does not clarify the focus's faith call or final condemnation.
The tranquil soul is a limited positive contrast to the self-hating soul at judgment.
Those who reject revelation are shown standing before their Lord and blaming one another for lost faith.
The warning of the Day of Meeting establishes the same approaching judgment setting.
They return to themselves and acknowledge their own wrongdoing, closely paralleling self-directed blame.
Recitation and prayer do not develop the focus's refused faith call or judgment-time reproach.
Noah's grateful servanthood does not clarify the focus's call, disbelief, or condemnation.
The joining of souls is only general eschatological background for the focus's final scene.
Disbelievers deny the Hour, whose certain arrival provides the setting for the focus's later rebuke.
It declares disbelievers destined for the Fire, directly extending the focus's judgment verdict.
On the Day of Judgment, false deification is exposed before God's complete knowledge.
The believers' promised desires in the hereafter do not clarify the focus's rejected call and remorse.
Individual guidance or misguidance returns upon oneself, and punishment follows only after a messenger is sent.
The command to call for many destructions portrays the despair of the condemned at final punishment.
Its distinction between outward submission and faith entering the heart sharpens the focus's issue of genuine belief.
When God's command comes, judgment is decided in truth and the falsifiers lose.
Calling to the good gives a communal positive counterpart to the focus's rejected invitation to faith.
Hidden hostility in an inner circle does not clarify the focus's faith call or final self-reproach.
Divine dislike of arrogance lightly supports the moral gravity of the focus's condemnation.
A people change what is within themselves before a blessing is changed, linking inward response to consequence.
Those who do not believe are deaf to the revelation and called from a distant place.
The chains and dragging describe the punishment sequence that follows the focus's verdict.
Faithful striving with wealth and selves is only a broad positive contrast to disbelief.
Revelation guides to the straight path and gives the content of the faith invitation refused in the focus.
The declaration of one God and command to submit directly states the faithful alternative to disbelief.
False partners are called but do not answer as their devotees see punishment.
The challenge to call an assembly does not clarify the focus's divine call or judgment.
The warning of the near Day and absence of accepted intercession directly frames the focus's judgment scene.
Zechariah's personal prayer for offspring does not clarify the focus's refused call to faith.
Its use of mqt for a prohibited practice adds the term's severe moral valence.
The question about a missing item does not clarify faith, self-reproach, or final judgment.
Forgetting God causes people to forget themselves, closely supporting the focus's self-directed loss and hatred.
The call to Abraham in the sacrifice narrative does not clarify the focus's faith call or condemnation.
At judgment, alleged partners provide no intercession and their devotees disown them.
Every self is held in pledge for what it earned, supporting the focus's personal accountability.
Calling the Prophet from outside his rooms does not clarify the focus's call to faith.
Messengers bring clear proofs before criminals are punished, connecting rejected guidance to consequence.
God answers the caller and immediately commands people to answer Him and believe, directly mirroring the focus.
Mocking the messenger while disbelieving in the Merciful gives a clear form of rejecting revelation.
Moses's momentary inward fear does not clarify the focus's faith call or final self-reproach.
Disbelievers are rebuked for verses recited to them, arrogance, and criminal refusal.
The condemned admit that messengers brought clear proofs, yet their later calls are declared futile.
Disbelievers return to God to be told of their deeds, including what lies within their breasts.
Breaking a covenant harms one's own self, a limited parallel to self-incurred consequence.
A household invitation and visiting etiquette do not clarify the focus's faith call or final judgment.
The legal procedure for spousal accusation does not clarify the focus's themes.
The command to believe in God and His messengers supplies the positive response to the focus's rejected call.
The believers' prior calling upon God is a limited positive contrast to refusing the call to faith.
Prayer times do not clarify the focus's disbelief, self-hatred, or final rebuke.
Every community is called to its record and repaid for its deeds, directly detailing final accountability.
Inheritance allocations do not clarify the focus's faith call or judgment-time condemnation.
Crisis prayer followed by disregard shows a broader pattern of calling and then turning away.
Family nursing and support rules do not clarify the focus's call to faith or final judgment.
Protecting selves and families from the Fire gives a direct preventive counterpart to final condemnation.
The condemned confess their sins and ask whether any exit remains, directly continuing the focus's self-reproach.
The believing man warns of a coming day of mutual calling, extending the focus's final summons.
It explicitly names the Day of Calling, the judgment setting in which the focus's address is heard.
Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire before their final entry into the greatest torment.
The Fire's inhabitants dispute with one another, giving a nearby form of post-judgment blame.
The condemned call the keepers of Hell after clear proofs had already reached them.
The Day when wrongdoers have no excuse reinforces the irreversibility of the focus's verdict.
Those who deny the Book and the messages brought by messengers are led into the punishment sequence.
The condemned are dragged through boiling water after the focus's declaration of God's hatred.
They are confronted with the partners they had associated besides God, exposing their prior disbelief.
The command to enter Hell eternally gives the outcome of the condemned addressed in the focus.
Followers wish for a return to disown their leaders after bonds break, a close counterpart to irrevocable regret.
Those facing the Fire wish they could return and not deny their Lord's signs.
Standing before their Lord exposes the rejected meeting with God as truth.
Those who deny the meeting with God bear their burdens when the Hour arrives suddenly.
Those who deny God's signs and reject them arrogantly are named companions of the Fire.
When fulfillment arrives, deniers ask for an impossible return and are said to have lost themselves.
Evil-doers face darkened faces and abiding Fire, providing a visual judgment counterpart.
The rejecters' impossible ransom and evil accounting clarify the final cost of denial.
All appear before God and the weak blame the arrogant leaders who led them astray.
Wrongdoers ask for a brief delay so they may answer the call, directly echoing the missed response in the focus.
When witnesses are raised, disbelievers are neither permitted excuse nor restored to favor.
Seeing the punishment leaves wrongdoers without reprieve or delay.
Those who disbelieve in God's signs are gathered blind, deaf, and mute into Hell.
Those who disbelieve are offered the Fire, whose enclosure and drink portray the consequence of refusing truth.
At death, the sinner asks to be returned to perform righteousness, a direct form of belated recognition.
The condemned admit that misery overcame them and that they became a people astray.
They ask to be brought out of the Fire so that changed conduct might prove repentance.
The wrongdoer bites his hands in regret for not taking the messenger's way.
He laments taking a companion who diverted him from the reminder after it came.
The remembrance was available, but Satan's misleading is recognized only after the loss.
Those who disbelieve in God's signs and meeting despair of mercy and receive painful punishment.
Sinners bow their heads before their Lord and ask to return after finally seeing and hearing.
Each attempted escape from the Fire ends in return to the punishment they had denied.
God curses disbelievers and prepares a blazing Fire for them.
As their faces are turned in the Fire, they wish they had obeyed God and the messenger.
Disbelievers in the Fire ask for death, but neither death nor mitigation is granted.
They cry to be brought out to act righteously after rejecting the earlier warning.
The command to enter Hell identifies it as the Fire repeatedly denied in earthly life.
Entry into the Fire is explicitly tied to persistent disbelief.
The soul laments its neglect toward God and its former mockery.
It wishes it had received guidance so as to be among the God-conscious.
Seeing punishment, it asks for another return in order to do good.
God answers that His signs had come, but they were denied with arrogance and disbelief.
Disbelievers are driven to Hell and rebuked for rejecting messengers and warnings.
The command to enter Hell eternally gives the final destination of those who refused faith.
Neither endurance in the Fire nor appeal for reconciliation changes the condemned outcome.
The Fire's inhabitants ask to see those who led them astray, shifting regret into blame.
The wrongdoers see the punishment in humiliation and recognize the truly ruined at resurrection.
The guilty remain in Hell, despaired of relief.
The inhabitants of Hell call for death after their Lord's judgment has become fixed.
They are rebuked because the promise and Hour were true, but they denied or doubted them.
The evil of their deeds becomes clear and the punishment they mocked encloses them.
They are told they are forgotten as they forgot their meeting with this Day.
Mocking God's signs and being deceived by worldly life explains why no exit from the Fire remains.
The obstinate disbeliever is commanded into Hell after resisting good and remaining in doubt.
The guilty are driven violently toward the Fire on the Day of judgment.
No ransom is accepted from hypocrites or disbelievers; the Fire is their final refuge.
Disbelievers are told not to make excuses because they are repaid only for what they did.
Those who disbelieve in their Lord receive Hell, explicitly naming the evil destination.
Hell's raging sound supplies the sensory setting for the focus's condemnation.
Hell nearly bursts with rage as each group of disbelievers is cast into it.
The condemned admit that a warner came, but they denied him and rejected the warning.
They confess that hearing or reasoning rightly would have kept them from the Fire.
They confess their sin, directly linking recognition of guilt to the companions of the Blaze.
The one given his record in the left hand laments the final disclosure of his account.
His former authority has vanished, a concise image of final loss after judgment.
The wrongdoer sees what his hands sent ahead and wishes he were dust.
